abstract: Adult fibromyalgia (FM) is characterized by altered functional connectivity between sensory, salience, and default mode networks (DMN), yet its early emergence and hierarchical organization remain unclear in Juvenile Fibromyalgia (JFM). We used stepwise functional connectivity (SFC) to detect early changes in the hierarchical integration of sensory signals toward salience and heteromodal networks in adolescents with JFM. Additionally, we assessed whether these alterations overlap with FM-associated gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Forty-six adolescent females with JFM (16.44-1.11 years) and forty-three healthy females (16.09-1.06 years) completed clinical questionnaires and underwent resting-state fMRI. Whole-brain voxel-wise SFC mapped connectivity patterns from primary sensory regions (visual, somatosensory, auditory) toward the DMN across increasing link-step distances. Regression models examined associations between symptom severity and SFC measures. Spatial overlap between functional findings and FM-associated gene expression profiles was also evaluated. Both groups showed a similar pattern, progressing from primary to secondary sensory regions, then to multimodal integration and salience areas, and finally to heteromodal DMN cortices. Greater symptom severity was associated with reduced second-step connectivity between secondary somatosensory cortices and the right anterior insula/operculum (T=5.11, pFWE<0.05). The neuronal transcription factor MYT1L showed relatively higher expression in AHBA in an overlapping region including the pars opercularis. Large-scale sensory-to-heteromodal functional architecture appears preserved in JFM. However, patients with greater symptom burden show reduced propagation of somatosensory information toward salience-interoceptive regions, suggesting altered multimodal processing. This disruption spatially overlaps with MYT1L expression, pointing towards a developmentally sensitive circuit vulnerability in severe patients.
